comment: What must not silently disappear from gmailtriage. `prose` names guardrails no code enforces; `split` declares which half of the skill is deterministic; `baseline` names the offline, $0 checks pinned against a real run.

prose.pattern: A message is trashed only because a rule the user wrote matc
prose.rationale: The one rule. It is the reason this skill exists rather than a prompt; lose the line and the skill becomes a generic assistant with extra steps.

prose.pattern: Never claim a result you did not observe
prose.rationale: Honesty about what was verified is the whole house contract. A skill that reports success it did not witness is worse than one that reports nothing.

prose.pattern: Never trash a thread the plan did not name
prose.rationale: The scaffolded invariant here was about a detect step this skill does not have. This is the one that matters: the plan is the authorisation, and a thread outside it has no rule behind it. Lose this line and `apply` becomes advisory.

prose.pattern: Never move a thread the plan did not name, and never under an action it did
prose.rationale: The sort half of the one rule. A plan that authorises filing a thread into a folder must not equally authorise trashing it — same thread id, same plan, catastrophically different outcome. Lose this line and the two actions collapse into one permission, which is how sorting becomes a way around every trash guard in the skill.

prose.pattern: Never invent a folder name silently
prose.rationale: Naming an unhoused cluster is the one judgment call sorting adds, and it belongs to the user. A skill that guesses files a school district into a folder named after its mail vendor, and mail the user cannot find is mail the user has lost.

Trash is recoverable for 30 days and the MCP has no permanent delete. Calling it deletion overstates the risk to the user and, worse, invites someone to 'fix' the skill by reaching for a destructive operation that does not exist. Since 0.2.0 the same line covers archiving, which is not destructive at all.

prose.pattern: Never name a sub-label after the sender when the sender hosts mail
prose.rationale: Splitting a folder into sub-labels re-opens the exact failure the folder-naming rule closed: an applicant tracking system, a signing service or an invoicing platform sends for whoever bought it, so the address names the vendor and the subject names the organisation. Lose this line and `Recruiting/Ashbyhq` files every employer into one folder — the school-district-under-its-mail-vendor bug, committed by the fix for it.

prose.pattern: Never let a broad rule stand in front of a rule filing into a sub-label
prose.rationale: This pair does not fail, it drifts — fresh mail takes the parent rule and mail already filed skips it and takes the child, so which folder a thread lands in depends only on when it arrived and nothing reports it. Lose this line and nesting silently produces two half-filled folders out of one rule set.

prose.pattern: the guard is on what the skill suggests
prose.rationale: The withheld list is about what the skill proposes, never about what the user may decide. Losing the distinction turns a helpful default into a tool that argues with its owner.

deterministic.step: report whether this mailbox has any rules yet, and the single next thing to do — the only command safe to run before anything is configured
cluster a real inbox sample into trash candidates and sort candidates, matching each sort cluster against the labels the mailbox already has

cluster a folder that already has mail in it by sender domain, match each cluster against the sub-labels that folder already has, flag the senders that host mail for many organisations, and say when the folder is still one thing

validate and store rules, compiling each to a Gmail query and refusing one that is malformed, matches everything, matches nothing, files into a label Gmail owns, or stands in front of a rule filing into a sub-label of its own destination
reconcile every folder the rules file into against the mailbox's real labels, and refuse to pass until each one exists

evaluate the stored rules against a named slice of the mailbox — the inbox by default, or a folder already filed — and enumerate exactly which threads each rule would take, every label each one applies, which of those the thread does not already carry, and which leave the inbox, without touching any of them
authorise exactly the threads the plan named, per action, refuse anything it did not, and write a receipt of every move
reverse every move listed in a previous run's receipt — untrash, unlabel, and put back in the inbox

nondeterministic.step: decide which proposed rules are actually safe to accept, and which cluster is a newsletter the user genuinely reads
nondeterministic.why: a sender sending fifty near-identical bulk messages looks the same whether it is a retailer the user ignores or the school district they need; only the user knows which

nondeterministic.step: name a folder for a cluster that has no existing home
nondeterministic.why: a folder name is a decision about how the user already thinks — whether their word is "Shopping" or "Retail", whether the bank goes under "Finance" or its own name — and nothing in the mail says it; a script that guesses files a school district under its mail vendor

nondeterministic.step: name the organisation behind a sender that hosts mail for many of them
nondeterministic.why: an applicant tracking system, a signing service and an invoicing platform all send on behalf of whoever bought them, so the address names the vendor and the subject names the organisation; no-reply@ashbyhq.com is Obvious in one thread and someone else in the next, and only reading the subject says which

nondeterministic.step: decide whether a folder is several things or still one
nondeterministic.why: four employers in Recruiting want splitting and four notices from one bank in Statements do not, and the counts look identical either way; a sub-label holding everything its parent holds has given one pile two names rather than organising anything

nondeterministic.step: word each rule so a reader six months later can tell what it was meant to catch
nondeterministic.why: a Gmail query is precise and unreadable, and a rule nobody can interpret is a rule nobody will dare to edit

nondeterministic.step: judge when a plan looks wrong and should be questioned rather than applied
nondeterministic.why: a rule that suddenly matches ten times its usual volume is either a sender gone rogue or a rule that drifted, and nothing in the count itself says which

_baseline_comment: Pinned against a real run of this skill, never a synthetic fixture. Offline and $0 by construction: no network, no model, so CI cannot spend and cannot flake.

baseline.rationale: the rule compiler or the planner silently changing which threads a rule takes, while still emitting a complete-looking plan — pinned against a real triage run over a frozen, redacted corpus of this account's own threads — propose, rules and plan re-run and byte-compared.
the one rule failing silently — the model, or a bug, trashing something no rule named — pinned against a receipt-producing apply run handed a thread id absent from its plan.
a malformed or over-broad rule reaching apply, which is how one bad rule empties an inbox — pinned against a rule whose compiled query is empty or matches the entire mailbox.

sorting becoming a way around every trash guard in the skill — a rule declaring {"action":"label","label":"TRASH"} destroys mail through the one action that exists so nothing is destroyed, and no trash guard is looking at a label rule. Pinned against a rule set naming TRASH, SPAM and CATEGORY_PROMOTIONS as destinations.

the two actions collapsing into one permission — a plan that authorises filing a thread into a folder must not authorise trashing it, since it is the same thread id in the same plan with a catastrophically different outcome. Pinned against a real plan whose label-rule thread ids are handed to apply as a trash list.

the sub-label half silently ceasing to work — pinned against a real retroactive run over this account's own Recruiting folder: subdivide clustering it, and plan re-evaluating the rules against `label:Recruiting` rather than the inbox, both re-run and byte-compared. Catches a cluster losing its home, a vendor-hosted sender being auto-named after its vendor, the parent label dropping out of a sub-label's path, and the retroactive plan reporting archives it would never perform.

a retroactive pass that never finishes — re-planning the frozen Recruiting folder with its sub-labels already applied must take ZERO threads. If label ids stop resolving to names, or the already-filed short-circuit stops firing, every run re-proposes everything the last one filed and the skill silently never converges while every table still looks correct.

the drift that nesting invites — a rule filing into a folder standing ahead of one filing into a sub-label of it does not fail, it splits the mailbox by arrival time. Pinned two-sided against a rule set carrying that exact pair, which must be refused, and the corrected set, which must pass — so the check cannot be satisfied by refusing nesting outright.

a fixture refresh collapsing the corpus to a handful of threads, so the golden passes over almost nothing — pinned against the frozen thread corpus, label list and rule set, with a declared minimum count.
